title: Cardiac arrest and post-ROSC care
summary: Run high-quality CPR and ALS for shockable and non-shockable rhythms, find and fix the Hs and Ts, manage peri-arrest rhythms, then deliver a structured post-ROSC bundle, fever prevention and safe multimodal neuroprognostication.

topics.title: Recognition and high-quality CPR
topics.summary: Recognise arrest in under 10 s, start compressions immediately at 100-120/min and 5-6 cm depth, attach the defibrillator, and protect compression fraction.

steps.title: Recognise arrest
steps.detail: Unresponsive and not breathing normally (gasping = arrest). Check for a carotid pulse for no more than 10 s. If in doubt, start CPR.

steps.title: Call for help and the defibrillator
steps.detail: Shout for help, call the arrest team (in hospital) and bring the defibrillator/AED and arrest trolley. Note the time.

steps.title: Start chest compressions
steps.detail: Lower half of the sternum, 100-120/min, 5-6 cm deep, full recoil, minimal leaning. Firm surface (CPR board or bed CPR mode).

steps.title: Ventilate 30:2
steps.detail: Bag-valve-mask with 100% O2 and an oropharyngeal airway: 2 breaths over ~1 s each with visible chest rise, then 30 compressions.

steps.title: Continuous compressions
steps.detail: Once intubated or SGA placed: continuous compressions and 1 breath every 6 s (10/min). Confirm tube with waveform capnography.

steps.title: Attach pads and analyse
steps.detail: Pads on during compressions (right infraclavicular + left mid-axillary V6, or antero-posterior). Pause ≤ 10 s for rhythm check.

steps.title: Swap compressors and check
steps.detail: Change compressor at each rhythm check to avoid fatigue. Aim for a compression fraction > 80%.

steps.title: Monitor CPR quality
steps.detail: Waveform ETCO2: aim ≥ 10 mmHg and ideally ≥ 20 mmHg; a sudden rise (often > 10 mmHg jump) suggests ROSC. Arterial diastolic pressure if an arterial line is in place.

tables.title: High-quality CPR targets
rows: < 10 s for rhythm or pulse check, pre-shock pause < 5 s
Long pauses for intubation or IV access
Falling ETCO2 = tiring compressor or poor CPR

redFlags.text: Agonal gasping is cardiac arrest: start CPR.
ETCO2 persistently < 10 mmHg in an intubated patient: improve compressions, check tube position, look for a cause.
Pre-shock pause > 5 s or pauses for intubation: re-plan the team.

pitfalls.text: Spending > 10 s searching for a pulse.
Hyperventilation with the bag: raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return.
Compressing on a soft ICU mattress without activating the CPR function.

pearls.text: Assign roles early: leader, compressors (2-3), airway, defibrillator, drugs, recorder/timer.
Indian Resuscitation Council (IRC) teaches compression-only life support (COLS) to lay rescuers; in hospital use full CCLS/ACLS.

algorithm.title: Arrest recognition to first rhythm check

nodes.text: Collapsed or unresponsive patient
Ensure safety; shout for help
Breathing normally / definite pulse within 10 s?
Not in arrest: ABCDE, recovery position or rapid response
Call arrest team, bring defibrillator
Attach pads during CPR; pause ≤ 10 s for rhythm check
Go to ALS: shockable or non-shockable pathway

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Compressions generate cardiac output by direct cardiac and thoracic pump effects, producing at best 25-30% of normal output. Coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic minus right atrial pressure) above ~15-20 mmHg is linked to ROSC, and it falls within seconds of stopping compressions. That is why pauses are so harmful.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- AHA 2025 BLS and ERC 2025 BLS keep 100-120/min and 5-6 cm depth with full recoil.
- AHA 2025 ALS: 10 breaths/min with an advanced airway; waveform capnography is recommended to confirm and monitor tube placement; ETCO2 or arterial diastolic pressure may be used to monitor CPR quality; head-up CPR is not recommended outside trials.
- Compression fraction > 60-80% and shorter peri-shock pauses are associated with better survival in observational data.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Optimal ventilation strategy before an advanced airway (30:2 vs continuous compressions with asynchronous breaths).
- Mechanical CPR devices are not better than good manual CPR, but help during transport, PCI or prolonged resuscitation.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- The Indian Resuscitation Council (IRC, a joint initiative led by the Indian Society of Anaesthesiologists) published BCLS and CCLS guidelines in 2017 adapted to Indian settings, and promotes compression-only life support for lay rescuers.
- Many Indian wards lack AEDs; place defibrillators on every floor and train nurses to defibrillate before the doctor arrives.

quiz.stem: What compression rate and depth are recommended for adult CPR?
quiz.explanation: 100-120/min at 5-6 cm depth with full recoil.

quiz.stem: Once an endotracheal tube is placed during CPR, ventilation should be:
options: 1 breath every 6 s with continuous compressions
quiz.explanation: With an advanced airway, give 10 breaths/min without pausing compressions.

quiz.stem: During CPR the ETCO2 suddenly rises from 14 to 38 mmHg. Most likely?
quiz.explanation: An abrupt rise in ETCO2 suggests return of spontaneous circulation; check rhythm and pulse at the next check.

topics.title: ALS: shockable rhythms (VF / pulseless VT)
topics.summary: Shock early, resume CPR immediately for 2 min, give adrenaline after initial shocks fail and amiodarone (or lidocaine) for persisting VF, and treat the cause.

steps.title: Shock immediately
steps.detail: Biphasic at the manufacturer's recommended energy (commonly 150-200 J; if unknown use maximum). Resume CPR immediately without pulse check.

steps.title: Rhythm check → 2nd shock
steps.detail: Still VF/pVT: shock (same or higher energy), resume CPR. Get IV access (IO if IV fails).

steps.title: 3rd shock, then drugs
steps.detail: After the 3rd shock: adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV (ERC timing). AHA: adrenaline after initial defibrillation attempts fail; amiodarone or lidocaine for shock-refractory VF.

steps.title: Repeat adrenaline
steps.detail: 1 mg every alternate 2-min cycle.

steps.title: Second antiarrhythmic dose
steps.detail: Amiodarone 150 mg (or lidocaine 0.5-0.75 mg/kg).

steps.title: Optimise and think
steps.detail: Check pad contact and position, consider antero-posterior pads (vector change); check K+, Mg2+, ischaemia; consider early PCI or ECPR where available. VC and double sequential defibrillation are not established (AHA 2025).

steps.time: Monitored, witnessed VF in ICU or cath lab
steps.title: Up to 3 stacked shocks
steps.detail: If pads are already on, give up to three quick successive shocks before starting compressions (ERC).

doseCards.dose: 1 mg every 3-5 min, starting after the 3rd shock (ERC)
doseCards.dilution: 1 mL of 1 mg/mL ampoule, or 10 mL of 100 mcg/mL

doseCards.dose: 300 mg after 3rd shock; 150 mg after 5th shock
doseCards.dilution: 150 mg/3 mL ampoules: 300 mg = 6 mL; may dilute to 20 mL D5

doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg: 100 mg (5 mL of 2%), then 50 mg

redFlags.text: Polymorphic VT is always unstable: unsynchronised shock immediately (AHA 2025).
Recurrent VF after ROSC: correct K+ (aim 4-4.5) and Mg2+, give amiodarone infusion, urgent cardiology for ischaemia.

pitfalls.text: Pausing CPR to check a pulse straight after the shock: resume compressions first.
Charging the defibrillator with compressions stopped: charge during compressions.
Synchronised mode left on for VF: the defibrillator will not fire.

pearls.text: Most VF seen at the next rhythm check is recurrent VF after a successful shock, not shock failure (AHA 2025).
In India, consider hyperkalaemia, organophosphate and aluminium phosphide poisoning as causes of refractory arrhythmia.

nodes.text: Rhythm check: VF or pulseless VT
Shock (biphasic 150-200 J or maximum)
CPR 2 min immediately; IV/IO access; airway when it does not interrupt CPR
Rhythm check: still VF/pVT?
Is this after the 3rd shock or later?
Adrenaline 1 mg every 3-5 min; amiodarone 300 mg (150 mg after 5th shock)
Organised rhythm with pulse or ETCO2/arterial waveform?
Go to non-shockable pathway
ROSC: go to post-ROSC bundle

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **AHA 2025:** biphasic preferred; single shocks rather than stacked; manufacturer energy (maximum if unknown); higher energy for subsequent shocks may be considered. Adrenaline 1 mg every 3-5 min; in shockable rhythms after initial defibrillation attempts fail. Amiodarone or lidocaine may be considered for shock-refractory VF/pVT. Routine calcium, bicarbonate and magnesium are not recommended.
- **ALPS (2016):** amiodarone and lidocaine did not improve survival to discharge overall, but improved survival in bystander-witnessed arrests.
- **PARAMEDIC2 (2018):** adrenaline improved 30-day survival but not favourable neurological survival.
- **DOSE-VF (2022):** vector change and double sequential defibrillation improved survival in refractory VF by intention-to-treat; AHA 2025 judges usefulness "not established" given methodological concerns.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Adrenaline timing in VF differs slightly between AHA ("after initial shocks fail") and ERC ("after the 3rd shock").
- Double sequential defibrillation risks defibrillator damage and requires millisecond timing.
- ECPR for refractory VF needs a system (rapid transport, cannulation team) that very few Indian centres have.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Biphasic defibrillators are now standard in most Indian ICUs; older monophasic units (360 J) may still be found in smaller hospitals.
- Lidocaine for IV use must be the preservative-free plain 2% preparation; avoid adrenaline-containing local anaesthetic vials.

quiz.stem: According to ERC, when is the first adrenaline given in VF arrest?
quiz.explanation: ERC gives adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg after the 3rd shock; AHA says after initial defibrillation attempts fail.

quiz.stem: What is the second dose of amiodarone in refractory VF?
quiz.explanation: 300 mg first, then 150 mg after the 5th shock.

quiz.stem: Immediately after delivering a shock, you should:
quiz.explanation: Resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes; pulse checks come at the next rhythm check.

quiz.stem: AHA 2025 says polymorphic VT should be treated with:
quiz.explanation: Sustained polymorphic VT cannot be synchronised reliably and is always unstable: defibrillate.

topics.title: ALS: PEA, asystole and the reversible causes (Hs and Ts)
topics.summary: Give adrenaline as soon as possible, keep CPR going, and actively search for and treat the 4 Hs and 4 Ts, using POCUS only without interrupting compressions.

steps.title: Confirm PEA or asystole
steps.detail: Check leads, gain and pads; fine VF can look like asystole. Continue CPR.

steps.title: Adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO
steps.detail: As soon as access is available, then every 3-5 min.

steps.title: Rhythm check
steps.detail: Shockable → shock pathway. Organised rhythm → pulse check. Otherwise continue CPR.

steps.title: Work through Hs and Ts
steps.detail: Use history, ABG/VBG (K+, pH, glucose, Hb), ETCO2 and POCUS during the pulse check, without prolonging pauses.

steps.title: Treat the cause
steps.detail: Hyperkalaemia: calcium + insulin-dextrose + bicarbonate; tension: needle/finger thoracostomy; tamponade: pericardiocentesis; PE: thrombolysis; hypovolaemia: fluids/blood; toxins: antidotes.

steps.title: Continue CPR 60-90 min
steps.detail: After fibrinolysis for PE, continue resuscitation for 60-90 min before stopping.

steps.title: Decide on continuing
steps.detail: Consider cause, ETCO2 trend (persistently < 10 mmHg after 20 min of ALS in an intubated patient supports stopping as part of a multimodal decision), comorbidity, and wishes.

doseCards.dose: Calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL (or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL)
doseCards.notes: Not routine in arrest; separate line from bicarbonate.

doseCards.dose: 50 mg bolus; consider repeat 50 mg after 15 min

doseCards.verify: Extrapolated from STEMI dosing; confirm local protocol.

tables.title: 4 Hs and 4 Ts: clues and treatment
rows: Respiratory arrest, blocked/displaced tube, low SpO2 before arrest
100% O2, confirm tube with capnography, DOPE check
Bleeding, GI loss, flat IVC, empty heart on POCUS
CKD, missed dialysis, peaked T, wide QRS; DKA; hypocalcaemia
Rewarm; ECPR if available; withhold drugs < 30 °C (ERC)
Ventilated, trauma, line insertion, absent breath sounds, no lung sliding
Needle or finger thoracostomy, then drain
Post-cardiac surgery, trauma, malignancy, effusion with RV collapse on POCUS
OP, aluminium phosphide, tricyclics, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, local anaesthetics
Specific antidotes (atropine, bicarbonate, calcium, high-dose insulin, lipid emulsion)
Dilated RV, DVT, chest pain, STEMI before arrest

redFlags.text: PEA with a dilated RV on POCUS and DVT risk: massive PE → thrombolyse.
Arrest in a dialysis patient: give calcium immediately; assume hyperkalaemia.
Arrest after central line insertion or in a ventilated patient: think tension pneumothorax.

pitfalls.text: Long POCUS pauses: AHA 2025 says POCUS may help only if it does not interrupt CPR.
Giving routine calcium or bicarbonate in every PEA: not recommended without a specific indication.
Calling asystole without checking leads and gain.

pearls.text: Pseudo-PEA (cardiac motion on echo without palpable pulse) has a better prognosis: treat aggressively and look hard for causes.
Narrow-complex PEA suggests a mechanical cause (tamponade, tension, PE, hypovolaemia); wide-complex PEA suggests metabolic or toxic causes (K+, sodium-channel blockers).

algorithm.title: Non-shockable rhythm loop with reversible causes

nodes.text: Rhythm check: PEA or asystole
CPR 2 min; IV/IO; adrenaline 1 mg ASAP then every 3-5 min
Look for Hs and Ts: gas, K+, glucose, POCUS during pauses, history
Specific cause found?
Targeted treatment (calcium, decompression, pericardiocentesis, thrombolysis, blood, antidote)
Rhythm at 2-min check?
Shockable: go to VF/pVT pathway
ROSC: post-ROSC bundle
Prolonged arrest with no reversible cause and ETCO2 < 10 after 20 min?
Consider stopping as a team decision; document; support family

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **AHA 2025:** adrenaline as soon as feasible in non-shockable rhythms. Routine calcium, bicarbonate and magnesium are not recommended. Pacing in established arrest is not recommended. POCUS for reversible causes "is not well established" and must not interrupt CPR. In intubated patients, ETCO2 ≤ 10 mmHg after 20 min of ALS may be one part of a multimodal decision to stop; never use ETCO2 alone in non-intubated patients.
- **ERC 2025 Special Circumstances:** detailed guidance on hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, PE, tamponade, toxins and other causes.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Bicarbonate in prolonged non-shockable arrest: observational signals but resuscitation-time bias; not recommended routinely.
- Termination of resuscitation rules are validated mainly in North American out-of-hospital settings, not in Indian in-hospital arrest.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Toxic causes are common in Indian ICUs: organophosphates, aluminium phosphide (celphos), yellow oleander, and snakebite with neuroparalysis (hypoxic arrest). See modules 28 and 29.
- Hyperkalaemia from missed dialysis and AKI is a frequent cause of PEA in Indian emergency departments.

quiz.stem: In asystole, adrenaline should be given:
options: As soon as IV/IO access is obtained
Only if POCUS shows cardiac standstill
quiz.explanation: In non-shockable rhythms, give adrenaline as soon as feasible.

quiz.stem: A patient on haemodialysis arrests with wide-complex PEA. First specific drug?
quiz.explanation: Presume hyperkalaemia: calcium stabilises the myocardium; then insulin-dextrose and bicarbonate.

quiz.stem: After thrombolysis for PE-related arrest, CPR should continue for at least:
quiz.explanation: Fibrinolytics need time to work; continue CPR 60-90 min.

quiz.stem: Which is NOT one of the 4 Ts?
quiz.explanation: The Ts are tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins and thrombosis.

topics.title: Peri-arrest rhythms: unstable tachycardia and bradycardia
topics.summary: Decide if the patient is unstable (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure). Unstable tachycardia: synchronised cardioversion. Unstable bradycardia: atropine, then adrenaline infusion or pacing.

steps.title: ABCDE, O2, IV, 12-lead ECG, monitor
steps.detail: Treat the patient, not the monitor. Ask: is the arrhythmia the cause of instability or a response to it (sepsis, bleeding, hypoxia)?

steps.title: Adverse features
steps.detail: Shock (SBP < 90 or MAP < 65, cold, confused), syncope, myocardial ischaemia, severe heart failure. Any = unstable.

steps.title: Synchronised cardioversion
steps.detail: Sedate if conscious (e.g. ketamine or small-dose propofol/midazolam). AF or flutter: start ≥ 200 J biphasic (AHA 2025). Regular narrow or monomorphic VT: 100-200 J, escalate. Up to 3 attempts, then amiodarone 300 mg over 10-20 min and repeat.

steps.title: Vagal then adenosine
steps.detail: Modified Valsalva (blow into a 10 mL syringe for 15 s then lie flat with legs raised), then adenosine 6 mg → 12 mg rapid push. See module 10 for full tachycardia care.

steps.title: Atropine
steps.detail: AHA: 1 mg IV every 3-5 min (max 3 mg). ERC: 500 mcg repeated to 3 mg. Indian ampoule 0.6 mg/mL.

steps.title: Adrenaline infusion or pacing
steps.detail: Adrenaline 2-10 mcg/min (or isoprenaline/dopamine) while arranging transcutaneous then transvenous pacing. Mobitz II, complete heart block with wide QRS, or asystole risk: pace early.

steps.title: Magnesium
steps.detail: 2 g IV over 10-15 min; correct K+; stop QT-prolonging drugs; overdrive pacing or isoprenaline if bradycardia-dependent.

doseCards.dose: AHA 1 mg every 3-5 min (max 3 mg); ERC 500 mcg every 3-5 min (max 3 mg)

doseCards.notes: 3 mg via central line or after heart transplant.

doseCards.role: After failed cardioversion, or stable VT
doseCards.dose: 300 mg over 10-20 min (ERC) or 150 mg over 10 min (AHA), then 900 mg over 24 h

redFlags.text: Irregular broad-complex tachycardia (pre-excited AF): no adenosine, verapamil, beta-blocker, digoxin or IV amiodarone; cardiovert.
Complete heart block with broad escape, Mobitz II or pauses > 3 s: pace early.
Sinus tachycardia in shock is compensation: do not cardiovert or rate-control it.

pitfalls.text: Cardioverting without the SYNC button (risk of R-on-T VF), or forgetting to re-select SYNC for each shock on some devices.

pearls.text: Transcutaneous pacing: set rate 60-70, increase current until electrical capture, then confirm mechanical capture with a femoral pulse; give analgesia.

nodes.text: Pulse present with abnormal rhythm
Adverse features? (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure)
Tachycardia or bradycardia?
Synchronised cardioversion (≥ 200 J for AF/flutter); amiodarone if it fails
Atropine; if no response adrenaline 2-10 mcg/min; pace
Stable: 12-lead ECG, identify rhythm, treat cause
Detailed management in module 10 (arrhythmias)
Rhythm controlled: monitor, correct K+ and Mg2+, find cause

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **AHA 2025 ALS:** stability assessment drives therapy. Synchronised cardioversion for unstable wide- or narrow-complex tachycardia. ≥ 200 J initial energy for AF and atrial flutter cardioversion. Adenosine for regular narrow-complex tachycardia; may be considered for stable regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia; never for unstable, irregular or polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia. Verapamil and diltiazem must not be given for wide-complex tachycardia.
- **ERC 2025:** atropine 500 mcg boluses for bradycardia; second-line drugs include isoprenaline and adrenaline; pacing for high-risk bradycardia.
consultantNotes.controversies: - Atropine dose difference (AHA 1 mg vs ERC 500 mcg). The app should state one unit protocol.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Atropine ampoules are 0.6 mg/mL in most Indian hospitals, so "1 mg" means 1.7 mL; mistakes are common.
- Isoprenaline availability varies; adrenaline infusion is the practical second line in most Indian ICUs.

quiz.stem: AHA 2025 recommends what initial energy for synchronised cardioversion of AF?
quiz.explanation: Higher first-shock energy (≥ 200 J biphasic) is preferred for AF and flutter.

quiz.stem: Adenosine is contraindicated in:
options: Stable regular monomorphic WCT for diagnosis
quiz.explanation: Adenosine can precipitate VF in pre-excited AF; cardiovert instead.

quiz.stem: An Indian ampoule of atropine is 0.6 mg/mL. How much for a 1 mg dose?

verify.reason: Availability and ampoule strength in India vary; not given a dose card here.

topics.title: Post-ROSC care: the first hours
topics.summary: Secure the airway, titrate oxygen to SpO2 92-98%, keep normocapnia and MAP ≥ 65 mmHg, get a 12-lead ECG, decide on angiography, find the cause, and plan temperature control and neuroprotection.

steps.title: Airway and breathing
steps.detail: Intubate if not already (RSI drugs at reduced doses; haemodynamics are fragile). Confirm with waveform capnography. Tidal volume 6-8 mL/kg PBW.

steps.title: Oxygen
steps.detail: 100% FiO2 until SpO2 is reliable, then titrate to SpO2 92-98% (AHA: 90-98%, PaO2 60-105 mmHg). Avoid hypoxaemia and hyperoxia.

steps.title: Ventilation
steps.detail: Normocapnia: PaCO2 35-45 mmHg. Remember PaCO2 runs above ETCO2 after arrest; check an ABG.

steps.title: Circulation
steps.detail: Arterial line. MAP ≥ 65 mmHg (ERC: > 65, SBP > 100). Fluids if preload-responsive, noradrenaline first-line, dobutamine for low output. Avoid hypotension.

steps.title: 12-lead ECG
steps.detail: STEMI or new LBBB with high suspicion → emergency coronary angiography.

steps.title: Find the cause
steps.detail: Echo; ABG, K+, glucose, troponin, lactate; CT head-to-pelvis (with CT pulmonary angiography) if no obvious cardiac cause (ERC).

steps.title: Angiography without STE
steps.detail: Not routinely emergent in stable comatose patients (COACT, TOMAHAWK). Go early if shock, electrical instability or ongoing ischaemia.

steps.title: Brain protection
steps.detail: Temperature control (next topic); short-acting sedation; glucose 140-180 mg/dL (70-180 per AHA); head up 30°; EEG if seizures suspected or patient sedated/paralysed.

steps.title: Organ support and family
steps.detail: Lung-protective ventilation, AKI monitoring, no routine prophylactic antibiotics or steroids. Early, honest communication with family; document the arrest timeline (no-flow, low-flow).

doseCards.dilution: Norad base 4 mg in 50 mL NS (80 mcg/mL); Indian ampoule 2 mg base/2 mL
doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg at 0.1 mcg/kg/min = 7 mcg/min = 420 mcg/h ÷ 80 = 5.25 mL/h
doseCards.verify: Indian labels may state noradrenaline bitartrate (4 mg bitartrate ≈ 2 mg base); confirm base vs salt.

doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg at 5 mcg/kg/min = 350 mcg/min = 21 000 mcg/h ÷ 5000 = 4.2 mL/h

redFlags.text: Recurrent VF/VT after ROSC: K+, Mg2+, ischaemia → cardiology now.
Persistent shock despite noradrenaline: echo for LV failure, tamponade, RV failure; think bleeding after CPR (liver/spleen injury).
STEMI on ECG: emergency PCI, even in a comatose patient.

pitfalls.text: Keeping FiO2 1.0 for hours after ROSC (hyperoxia).
Hyperventilating to 'correct' acidosis: causes cerebral vasoconstriction.
Early prognostic statements to family in the first 24 h.

pearls.text: BOX (2022): MAP 63 vs 77 mmHg and liberal vs restrictive O2 gave similar outcomes; so a 'safe' band, not a high target, is enough.
Record no-flow and low-flow times; they inform later prognostication and family conversations.

nodes.text: ROSC achieved
Airway, capnography, SpO2 92-98%, PaCO2 35-45, MAP ≥ 65
12-lead ECG: STEMI?
Emergency coronary angiography / PCI
Shock, electrical instability or suspected ongoing ischaemia?
Echo + CT head-to-pelvis (± CTPA) to find cause
Following commands?
ICU: temperature control, sedation, EEG, prognostication ≥ 72 h
Monitored care, treat cause, secondary prevention (ICD review)

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Post-cardiac arrest syndrome has four parts: brain injury, myocardial dysfunction (stunning, recovers over 24-72 h), systemic ischaemia-reperfusion response (sepsis-like vasoplegia), and the persisting precipitating cause.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **AHA 2025 post-cardiac arrest care:** SpO2 90-98%; normocapnia; avoid SBP < 90 and MAP < 65; emergency angiography for STEMI or shock/instability; head-to-pelvis CT and echo may be reasonable; no routine prophylactic antibiotics, steroids or seizure prophylaxis; routine MCS not recommended.
- **ERC-ESICM 2025:** SpO2 94-98%; normocapnia; MAP > 60-65; CT including CTPA when no cardiac cause; delay angiography in absence of STE unless coronary occlusion likely.
- **COACT (2019) and TOMAHAWK (2021):** immediate angiography did not improve survival in resuscitated patients without STE.
- **BOX (2022):** MAP target 63 vs 77 mmHg and restrictive vs liberal oxygen showed no difference in death or poor neurological outcome.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Exact oxygen target (90-98% vs 94-98%), and whether a higher MAP benefits chronic hypertensive patients.
- Mild hypercapnia (TAME 2023, not cited here) did not help.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Cath-lab access is limited outside metros; thrombolysis (tenecteplase) is reasonable for STEMI after ROSC if PCI cannot be done within 120 min, accepting the CPR-trauma bleeding risk. Discuss with cardiology.
- CT transfer of an unstable post-ROSC patient carries real risk in Indian hospitals without transport ventilators; use echo and bedside tests first.

quiz.stem: Which statement about coronary angiography after ROSC is correct?
options: All comatose patients need emergency angiography
Emergency angiography is indicated for STEMI or shock/electrical instability
Angiography is contraindicated in comatose patients
quiz.explanation: COACT and TOMAHAWK showed no benefit of routine immediate angiography without STE in stable patients.

quiz.stem: After ROSC, the ERC-ESICM SpO2 target is:
quiz.explanation: ERC-ESICM 2025 targets 94-98%; AHA 2025 accepts 90-98%.

quiz.stem: The BOX trial compared:
options: MAP 63 vs 77 mmHg and O2 targets
quiz.explanation: BOX tested blood pressure and oxygen targets in comatose survivors; neither changed outcome.

verify.reason: Practice point from STEMI guidelines; not a specific recommendation in the cited cardiac-arrest guidelines.

topics.title: Temperature control after cardiac arrest
topics.summary: In patients who remain comatose after ROSC, actively prevent fever (≤ 37.5 °C) for at least 72 h. Hypothermia at 32-36 °C is acceptable but not proven better.

steps.title: Identify eligible patients
steps.detail: Any adult not following commands after ROSC, regardless of rhythm or location.

steps.title: Measure core temperature
steps.detail: Bladder, oesophageal or blood (PA/femoral catheter) probe. Avoid axillary readings.

steps.title: Choose target
steps.detail: ERC-ESICM: actively prevent fever, keeping temperature ≤ 37.5 °C. AHA: choose and maintain a constant temperature between 32 and 37.5 °C.

steps.title: Devices
steps.detail: Feedback-controlled surface or intravascular device if available. Otherwise cold packs, cooling blankets, fans, paracetamol. No prehospital cold IV fluid boluses.

steps.title: Sedation and shivering
steps.detail: Short-acting sedation (propofol, fentanyl/remifentanil); manage shivering (Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale) with skin counter-warming, magnesium, opioids, dexmedetomidine; neuromuscular block as last resort.

steps.title: Duration
steps.detail: AHA: ≥ 36 h; ERC-ESICM: prevent fever for at least 72 h.

steps.title: Slow
steps.detail: If cooled below 36 °C: rewarm ≤ 0.25-0.5 °C/h; continue to prevent fever after rewarming. Do not actively rewarm patients with mild spontaneous hypothermia (32-36 °C) (ERC).

tables.title: Key temperature trials
rows: No difference in mortality or neurological outcome
Better neurological outcome at 90 days with 33 °C (10.2% vs 5.7%); fragile result
No difference in 6-month mortality; more arrhythmias with hypothermia

redFlags.text: Fever > 37.7 °C in a comatose post-arrest patient: treat promptly; it is associated with worse outcome.
Bradycardia < 40/min, arrhythmia or bleeding during hypothermia: consider warming to a higher target.

pitfalls.text: Stopping temperature control at 24 h and allowing rebound fever.
Unrecognised shivering raises metabolic rate and temperature: assess it every hour.

pearls.text: Hypothermia causes cold diuresis, hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia and slower drug clearance; rewarming causes K+ to rise.

nodes.text: ROSC, patient not obeying commands
Core temperature probe; sedation; arterial line
Current core temperature?
> 37.5 °C: active cooling (device, ice packs, blankets, paracetamol)
32-37.5 °C: do not actively rewarm; prevent fever
Hourly shivering check; counter-warming, magnesium, opioid, dexmedetomidine
≥ 72 h of fever prevention (AHA ≥ 36 h) and patient stable?
Continue fever prevention
Stop active control; keep monitoring for fever; proceed to prognostication

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **TTM2 (2021)** found no benefit of 33 °C over normothermia with active fever prevention.
- **HYPERION (2019)** suggested benefit for non-shockable rhythms; the ERC-ESICM 2025 guideline nevertheless recommends against routine active cooling and instead recommends fever prevention ≤ 37.5 °C for at least 72 h.
- **AHA 2025** still allows a deliberate constant target between 32 and 37.5 °C for at least 36 h.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Whether subgroups (severe brain injury, non-shockable, in-hospital arrest) benefit from deeper hypothermia.
- Device-based vs simple methods: feedback devices achieve targets better but outcome benefit is unproven.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Most Indian ICUs do not have feedback cooling devices; ice packs, cooling blankets, cold room air, fans and scheduled paracetamol are practical. Accept "fever prevention" as the realistic standard.
- Ambient temperatures above 35 °C in summer make passive fever prevention harder; plan for active measures.

quiz.stem: TTM2 compared 33 °C with:
quiz.explanation: TTM2 randomised 33 °C hypothermia vs normothermia with treatment of fever ≥ 37.8 °C; no difference.

quiz.stem: ERC-ESICM 2025 recommends fever prevention for at least:
quiz.explanation: Prevent fever (≤ 37.5 °C) for at least 72 hours in comatose survivors.

quiz.stem: Which is NOT recommended?
options: Prehospital rapid infusion of cold IV fluids
quiz.explanation: Prehospital cold fluid boluses increased pulmonary oedema and re-arrest without benefit.

verify.reason: AHA states avoid > 0.5 °C/h; many protocols use 0.25 °C/h.

topics.title: Neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest
topics.summary: Never decide on prognosis early. At ≥ 72 h after ROSC (and after sedation clears), combine examination, EEG, SSEP, NSE and imaging; poor outcome is likely only when two or more predictors agree.

steps.title: Do not prognosticate
steps.detail: Exclude confounders: sedatives, neuromuscular block, hypothermia, severe hypotension, hypoglycaemia, uraemia, hepatic failure.

steps.title: Collect data
steps.detail: Daily neurological exam (GCS motor, pupils, corneals, myoclonus). EEG (continuous or intermittent). NSE at 24, 48 and 72 h. SSEP at ≥ 24 h. CT brain early; MRI at 2-7 days.

steps.title: Assess unconscious patient
steps.detail: Consider prognostication in any patient not awake and obeying commands (GCS motor < 6) at ≥ 72 h, with no confounders.

steps.title: Look for ≥ 2 poor-outcome predictors
steps.detail: Bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes; bilaterally absent N20 SSEP; highly malignant EEG (suppressed background ± periodic discharges, or burst-suppression) > 24 h; NSE > 60 µg/L at 48 or 72 h; status myoclonus ≤ 72 h; diffuse anoxic injury on CT/MRI.

steps.title: Indeterminate if < 2
steps.detail: Continue support and reassess; look for favourable signs (motor withdrawal or better, NSE < 17 µg/L, continuous/reactive EEG, normal MRI).

steps.title: Shared decision
steps.detail: Multidisciplinary, documented, with family; separate brain death testing (module 21) from prognostication.

tables.title: Predictors of poor neurological outcome (ERC-ESICM 2025)
rows: Highly malignant pattern: suppressed background with or without periodic discharges, or burst suppression
Diffuse, extensive anoxic injury (loss of grey-white differentiation, diffusion restriction)

redFlags.text: Any prognostic statement before 72 h is unreliable unless brain death is confirmed.
Renal or hepatic failure delays clearance of midazolam and opioids; prognosticate later.

pitfalls.text: Using a single test (for example one absent pupillary reflex) to withdraw care.
Self-fulfilling prophecy: early pessimism leads to early withdrawal and confirms the prediction.

pearls.text: Myoclonus alone is not a reliable predictor; Lance-Adams syndrome (chronic post-hypoxic myoclonus) can occur with good cognition.
AHA 2025 also allows serum neurofilament light (NfL) as part of multimodal assessment where available.

nodes.text: Comatose ≥ 72 h after ROSC
Confounders excluded (sedation, temp, metabolic)?
Correct confounders; wait and reassess
Still not obeying commands (GCS motor ≤ 5)?
Obeying commands: no prognostication needed; rehabilitation
≥ 2 poor-outcome predictors present?
Poor outcome very likely: multidisciplinary discussion with family
Indeterminate: continue support, repeat assessment

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **ERC-ESICM 2025** extend prognostication to all unconscious patients (GCS motor ≤ 5, previously ≤ 3) and keep the multimodal strategy at ≥ 72 h with ≥ 2 concordant predictors of poor outcome; NSE > 60 µg/L at 48/72 h; favourable signs include NSE < 17 µg/L and continuous EEG background.
- **AHA 2025** endorses multimodal prognostication no earlier than 72 h after normothermia and sedation clearance; NSE and NfL may be used.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- NSE thresholds vary between analysers and studies; specificity is never 100%.
- Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy and organ donation pathways differ greatly between countries.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- SSEP, cEEG and NSE are unavailable in many Indian ICUs; rely on serial clinical examination, CT/MRI, and time. When tests are missing, be more conservative and allow longer observation.
- Families may need extended counselling; involve senior staff early. Indian law (Common Cause 2018 and 2023 modifications) allows withdrawal of life support with medical board process; see module 39.

quiz.stem: Earliest time for routine multimodal prognostication in a comatose survivor?
options: 72 h after ROSC and sedation clearance
quiz.explanation: At least 72 h, after excluding confounders.

quiz.stem: Which NSE value supports a poor outcome (ERC-ESICM 2025)?
quiz.explanation: NSE > 60 µg/L at 48/72 h is one predictor; NSE < 17 µg/L is favourable.

quiz.stem: How many concordant poor-outcome predictors are needed in the ERC-ESICM strategy?
quiz.explanation: Poor outcome is likely when two or more predictors are present.

verify.reason: Common Cause v Union of India (2018) and its 2023 modification; confirm details in module 39.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (epinephrine)
drugs.indications: All cardiac arrest rhythms; post-ROSC shock or symptomatic bradycardia as an infusion; anaphylaxis (IM).
drugs.adultDose: Arrest: 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 min (every second 2-min CPR cycle). Non-shockable: as soon as access is obtained. Shockable: after initial defibrillation attempts fail (ERC: after the 3rd shock; AHA: after initial shocks). Bradycardia or shock infusion: 2-10 mcg/min (≈ 0.02-0.15 mcg/kg/min).
drugs.preparationIndia: 1 mg/mL (1:1000) ampoules are standard in India. For arrest: give 1 mL undiluted and flush with 20 mL NS, or dilute 1 mg to 10 mL (100 mcg/mL). Infusion: 4 mg in 50 mL (80 mcg/mL).
drugs.cautions: High-dose adrenaline is not recommended. Tachyarrhythmias and hypertension after ROSC: stop the bolus schedule once ROSC is achieved.

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.indications: VF/pulseless VT persisting after shocks; stable VT; AF rate/rhythm control in the critically ill.
drugs.adultDose: Arrest: 300 mg IV/IO bolus after the 3rd shock, then 150 mg after the 5th shock (ERC); AHA: 300 mg then 150 mg. Stable VT or after ROSC: 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min for 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min for 18 h (max ~2.2 g/24 h).
drugs.preparationIndia: 150 mg/3 mL ampoules. In arrest, 300 mg (2 ampoules) can be pushed and flushed. Infusions must be made in 5% dextrose (e.g. 900 mg in 500 mL D5 or 300 mg in 50 mL D5 via central line).
drugs.cautions: Hypotension and bradycardia (polysorbate solvent); phlebitis peripherally; QT prolongation; long-term thyroid, liver and lung toxicity.

drugs.name: Lidocaine (lignocaine)
drugs.indications: Alternative to amiodarone for shock-refractory VF/pVT.
drugs.adultDose: 1-1.5 mg/kg IV/IO, then 0.5-0.75 mg/kg every 5-10 min if needed (max 3 mg/kg). Maintenance after ROSC 1-4 mg/min.
drugs.preparationIndia: 2% (20 mg/mL) preservative-free plain lignocaine for IV use (do NOT use the adrenaline-containing local anaesthetic vials).
drugs.cautions: CNS toxicity (seizures) and myocardial depression at high levels, especially in liver failure.

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.indications: Symptomatic or unstable bradycardia; organophosphate poisoning (very different doses, see module 28). Not used routinely in PEA/asystole.
drugs.adultDose: Bradycardia: AHA 1 mg IV every 3-5 min (max 3 mg); ERC 500 mcg IV, repeat every 3-5 min to max 3 mg.
drugs.preparationIndia: Commonly 0.6 mg/mL ampoules in India: 1 mg ≈ 1.7 mL, 0.5 mg ≈ 0.8 mL. Push fast and flush.
drugs.cautions: Often ineffective in heart transplant patients and in infranodal (Mobitz II / complete) block with wide QRS. Doses < 0.5 mg can cause paradoxical bradycardia.
drugs.verify: Confirm local ampoule strength (0.6 mg/mL vs 1 mg/mL).

drugs.name: Adenosine
drugs.indications: Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia; diagnostic in stable regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia.
drugs.adultDose: 6 mg rapid IV push with immediate 20 mL flush; if no effect 12 mg (AHA: may repeat 12 mg once; ERC: then 18 mg).
drugs.preparationIndia: 6 mg/2 mL vials. Use a large antecubital vein and a three-way tap for push-flush.
drugs.cautions: Avoid in asthma/severe bronchospasm, pre-excited AF, irregular or polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia. Reduce to 3 mg with central line, heart transplant, or dipyridamole/carbamazepine.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.indications: Torsades de pointes; documented hypomagnesaemia. Not routine in cardiac arrest.
drugs.adultDose: Torsades: 2 g IV over 1-2 min (arrest) or over 10-15 min (with pulse); may repeat once; then infusion 0.5-1 g/h if recurrent.
drugs.preparationIndia: 50% solution, 1 g in 2 mL ampoules (≈ 4 mmol Mg per g). 2 g = 4 mL; dilute in 10-20 mL NS for bolus.
drugs.cautions: Hypotension, flushing; caution in renal failure.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate 10% (or calcium chloride 10%)
drugs.indications: Cardiac arrest from hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia or calcium-channel-blocker overdose. NOT routine in arrest.
drugs.adultDose: Calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV (≈ 6.8 mmol Ca), or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL (≈ 6.8 mmol); repeat as needed.
drugs.preparationIndia: Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL ampoules are widely available; calcium chloride is less commonly stocked.
drugs.cautions: Do not give through the same line as bicarbonate (precipitates). Tissue necrosis with extravasation (especially chloride).

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.indications: Arrest due to hyperkalaemia or tricyclic/sodium-channel-blocker overdose. NOT routine in arrest.
drugs.adultDose: 50 mmol IV (≈ 50 mL of 8.4% or ≈ 56 mL of 7.5%), repeat according to blood gas.
drugs.preparationIndia: 7.5% (0.89 mmol/mL) and 8.4% (1 mmol/mL) 10 mL and 25 mL ampoules are both sold in India; check which you have.
drugs.cautions: Hypernatraemia, CO2 generation (ensure ventilation), inactivates catecholamines in the same line.

drugs.name: Alteplase
drugs.indications: Cardiac arrest with suspected or confirmed massive pulmonary embolism.
drugs.adultDose: Arrest from PE: 50 mg IV bolus (ERC); consider a further 50 mg after 15 min; continue CPR for 60-90 min after thrombolysis.
drugs.preparationIndia: 50 mg vials (Actilyse). Expensive; tenecteplase is often more available in Indian emergency departments.
drugs.cautions: Bleeding. Do not stop CPR early after giving a fibrinolytic.

drugs.name: Tenecteplase
drugs.indications: Alternative fibrinolytic for PE-related arrest when alteplase is unavailable (off-label for PE in many countries).
drugs.adultDose: Weight-based single bolus as for STEMI: < 60 kg 30 mg; 60-69 kg 35 mg; 70-79 kg 40 mg; 80-89 kg 45 mg; ≥ 90 kg 50 mg.
drugs.preparationIndia: 20 mg, 30 mg and 40 mg vials are marketed in India (including biosimilars).
drugs.verify: Use for PE arrest is extrapolated; confirm local protocol.

drugs.name: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine)
drugs.indications: Post-ROSC hypotension (MAP < 65 mmHg) after correcting volume.

drugs.name: Dobutamine
drugs.indications: Post-arrest myocardial dysfunction with low cardiac output.

verify.reason: Written against AHA 2025, ERC 2025 and ERC-ESICM 2025 post-resuscitation guidance (key recommendations read from the AHA guideline pages and published summaries). Where AHA and ERC differ, both are shown; the unit should choose one convention for the app.
Atropine is commonly 0.6 mg/mL in India; adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000); amiodarone 150 mg/3 mL; sodium bicarbonate 7.5% and 8.4% both exist. Confirm local stock before publishing dose volumes.
